A deeply unsettling robot dog bearing the eerily realistic face of Elon Musk was spotted mid-walkies on the streets of San Francisco this week. The robot is part of the Regular Animals project by Beeple, aka Mike Winkelmann, created in collaboration with mask-maker Hyperflesh and built on Unitree Go2 robot dogs. Art foundation NODE told WIRED the robots were taken out on a walk to promote Beeple’s upcoming exhibition in Palo Alto. Other versions of the robot dog feature the faces of Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Andy Warhol, Pablo Picasso, and Beeple himself.

Chinese robotics company AheadForm unveiled one of its most lifelike humanoid robot faces at WAIC 2026 in Shanghai. Unlike most humanoid robot demonstrations that focus on walking, running, lifting objects, or performing acrobatic moves, AheadForm showcased highly realistic facial interaction. The robot features natural blinking, eye contact, synchronized speech, subtle head movements, and expressive facial reactions designed to make conversations feel more human. According to the company, its self-supervised AI and high-precision bionic actuation enable coordinated movements of the eyes, mouth, face, and speech, creating a remarkably lifelike communication experience. The result is a humanoid face realistic enough to make people take a second look. #robotics #artificialintelligence #humanoidrobot #waic2026 #technology

Original Video Credit: IG/robotstory.ae Packed tightly inside its transport case, the humanoid robot begins unfolding its articulated limbs before extending both feet onto the floor. It then raises its torso, positions itself on the edge of the case, and transitions into a full standing posture without being physically lifted by a person. Coordinated electric joints and onboard control systems manage the sequence by continuously controlling limb positions and balance as the robot shifts its weight. Its arms and legs work together to create stable points of support while the body moves from a folded position to standing. Self-deployment demonstrates how humanoid robots can perform more than programmed walking or manipulation tasks. Being able to transition between complex body positions with minimal human assistance could make these machines easier to transport, deploy, and operate in real-world environments. XPENG’s humanoid robot, known as IRON, represents the company’s expansion beyond electric vehicles into robotics and embodied AI. XPENG, a Chinese EV manufacturer founded in 2014, has leveraged its expertise in electric drivetrains, AI software, and autonomous systems to develop robotic platforms capable of dynamic movement and real-time environmental interaction. Humanoid robots like IRON rely on advanced motion planning algorithms, electric actuators, and sensor fusion systems - typically combining cameras, LiDAR, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and force sensors. These systems allow the robot to maintain balance, adjust posture, and perform coordinated movements that appear fluid and human-like. Modern humanoid locomotion depends heavily on real-time feedback control. Small positional corrections are made hundreds of times per second to stabilize joints and prevent falls. This is similar to the control architecture used in self-balancing robots and autonomous vehicles. XPENG’s broader robotics initiative aligns with a global push toward general-purpose humanoid platforms - machines designed to operate in human environments rather than factory-only settings. While still in early development stages, such robots are being researched for applications ranging from logistics and manufacturing to service roles and human-robot interaction studies. videos.caption: I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

I'm sorry... but who looked at this and said, "Yep, that's the design!"? 🤣 If your rescue robot walks out of the woods looking like a seven-foot-tall mechanical demon carrying a chainsaw... maybe the branding department got a little carried away. 😂 They could have made it look like a normal industrial robot. Instead they named the company after a satyress (a mythical goat-like creature), gave it giant ram's horns, painted it matte black, and then acted surprised when the internet said, "What in the horror movie is THAT?" 😆 Sure, the company says the shape protects sensors and helps it work in dangerous environments. But let's be honest... the dramatic mythological look is also part of the branding. It gets people talking—and judging by all of us arguing about it, it worked. 😄 If I ever need rescuing in the woods and this thing comes walking toward me with glowing eyes... my first thought isn't going to be, "Thank goodness!" It's going to be, "Well... this is one interesting way to meet my maker." 🤣👹🤖
